sections.section_title: Initial Clinical Course: Sepsis and Disseminated Coagulopathy
sections.description: This section details the patient's initial presentation two days post-infection, focusing on the diagnosis of septic shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) driven by Capnocytophaga canimorsus. It explains the atypical rapid onset of symptoms and the initial clinical reasoning that prioritizes infection control over TMA before the case evolved.
subtopics: History of dog bite and delayed antibiotic initiation
Clinical signs of zoonotic sepsis: fever, hypoglycemia, septic shock
Development of pancytopenia and coagulopathy (DIC)
Initial differential diagnosis: Differentiating septic shock from malignancy or organ failure
Role of broad-spectrum antibiotics in early exposure management

sections.section_title: Diagnostic Reasoning: From Sepsis to Thrombotic Microangiopathy (TMA)
sections.description: This section covers the critical shift in clinical focus as the patient began to exhibit signs of renal failure and cytopenia not initially explained by sepsis alone. It outlines the systematic approach to ruling out common mimics (TTP, STEC-HUS) and the key diagnostic features (MAHA) that confirmed TMA.
subtopics: Signs of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA): Schistocytes and hemoglobin drop
Systematic exclusion of Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP) via ADAMTS13 activity
Exclusion of Shiga-toxin producing E. coli HUS via stool PCR
Renal biopsy findings: TMA features versus acute tubular necrosis
The impact of normal complement levels on diagnostic confidence in CM-HUS

sections.section_title: Pathophysiology: Complement Dysregulation and Infectious Triggers
sections.description: This section explains the biological mechanisms allowing a systemic infection to trigger complement-mediated HUS in an immunocompetent individual without prior genetic predisposition. It highlights the specific role of C. canimorsus and the paradox of complement activation during sepsis.
subtopics: Understanding Stability of Complement Components (C3/C4) in Acute HUS
Mechanism of C. canimorsus activation of the alternative complement pathway
Differentiating Acquired CM-HUS from Atypical HUS with Hereditary Complement Defects
The 'Second Hit' hypothesis: Infection as a trigger for complement cascade activation
Role of antibody-dependent cytotoxicity and schistocyte formation

sections.section_title: Therapeutic Strategy: Plasma Exchange and Eculizumab Implementation
sections.description: This section details the management decisions made in the inter-observation of sepsis and TMA resolution. It focuses on the specific choice of drugs (eculizumab vs. steroids), timing of intervention relative to infection clearance, and infection prevention measures.
subtopics: Bridging Therapy: Rationale for initial plasma exchange (PEX) before eculizumab
Timing of Eculizumab initiation relative to antibiotic efficacy
Risk stratification for eculizumab-associated infections (e.g., meningitis/neisseria)
Vaccination protocols: Prophylaxis for encapsulated bacteria
Clinical markers of therapeutic response: Platelet count and renal function

sections.section_title: Outcome, Follow-up, and Clinical Significance for Treating Rare Triggers
sections.description: This section summarizes the patient's recovery trajectory, renal recovery status, and longer-term implications for clinicians. It emphasizes the importance of recognizing rare presentations of TMA in the context of unusual infections.
subtopics: Assessment of renal function recovery: Dialysis dependence vs. recovery
Long-term trajectory of Complement Blockade therapy and cessation risks
Prophylactic management: Antibiotics during complement inhibition
Challenges in genetic testing for hereditary complement deficiencies in acute setting
Clinical lesson: TMA diagnosis can be obscured during septic phase
